Tết. Or Tết Nguyên Đán, meaning Festival of the First Morning, the Vietnamese New Year celebrated at the same moment as Chinese New Year, marking the start of the lunar calendar. The holiday spans several days and emphasizes family reunion, ancestor veneration, and renewal. It is the most important festival in Vietnamese culture, featuring special foods, cleaning rituals, and visits to temples and family shrines.

Tết is celebrated on the second new moon after the winter solstice, occurring on the same date as Chinese New Year in late January or February. The word Tết means festival, but Tết Nguyên Đán, or Tết of the first morning, is the primary New Year observance. Families prepare bánh chưng, which are square sticky rice cakes wrapped in dong leaves, and bánh dày, which are round glutinous rice cakes, both essential ceremonial foods.

Before Tết, homes are meticulously cleaned and decorated with yellow flowers such as hoa mai orchids or hoa đào peach blossoms. Ancestor altars are tended carefully, with families bringing offerings of fruit, flowers, incense, and food to honor the deceased. Children receive lì xì, lucky money in red envelopes, from elders, similar to Chinese hongbao. The first visitor to enter a home on New Year's Day is believed to influence the household's fortune for the year, and traditionally someone happy and successful is invited.
